Physical AI Architecture: The Ultimate 2026 VLA Engineering Guide
A deep technical analysis of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures, diffusion-based robot policies, and the infrastructure powering large-scale Physical AI systems.
by
External Sources & Technical References
This article is a technical deep-dive into the architecture and engineering of Physical AI systems in 2026. It covers the internals of Vision-Language-Action models, the full training pipeline from synthetic data generation to sim-to-real transfer, and the inference constraints governing edge deployment on current hardware. All specifications and benchmarks cited are drawn directly from NVIDIA’s published technical documentation, arXiv papers, and official developer blog posts.
TL;DR — Key Insights for AI Engineers
Physical AI is not a single model or framework — it is a multi-layer systems engineering challenge. The core problem is converting noisy, high-dimensional sensor input (RGB frames, depth maps, proprioceptive joint states, IMU readings) into continuous motor commands, in real time, across tasks and environments the system has never seen before. Every component in the stack is constrained by physics: the robot must maintain dynamic balance while manipulating objects, comply with joint torque limits, avoid collisions, and do all of this within the latency budget of a real-time control loop.
Before 2024, the dominant approach was task-specific policy learning: a robot was trained on demonstrations for a single task, in a single environment, with a fixed object set. Generalization was essentially absent. The architectural shift that defines 2025–2026 is the introduction of foundation model backbones into the policy — specifically, large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pretrained on internet-scale data — paired with action generation modules capable of producing smooth, continuous motor trajectories. This is the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) paradigm, and understanding its internals is prerequisite to evaluating any Physical AI platform.
VLA Architecture: Layer-by-Layer
Vision Encoder: SigLIP + MLP Projector
GR00T N1’s visual encoding pipeline begins with a SigLIP vision transformer. SigLIP — Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training — is a contrastive vision encoder trained to produce image representations that are semantically aligned with natural language descriptions. The SigLIP encoder in GR00T N1 operates on image patches of 14×14 pixels. For a standard input resolution, this produces a fixed-length sequence of visual tokens, each with an embedding dimension of 1152. The encoder comprises 27 SiglipEncoderLayer blocks, each containing a SiglipFlashAttention2 self-attention module (with query, key, and value projection dimensions of 1152), followed by layer normalization and a two-layer MLP with GELU activations and a hidden dimension of 4304.
In GR00T N1.6, the VLM was upgraded to a variant of Cosmos-Reason-2B with native resolution support — meaning the vision encoder processes images at their original aspect ratio rather than padding them to a square. This is architecturally significant: padding introduces artificial boundaries in the visual field that the attention mechanism can learn to attend to spuriously, degrading object localization and spatial reasoning. Native resolution support improves scene understanding and task decomposition reliability, particularly for manipulation tasks requiring fine-grained spatial judgment (e.g., grasping a specific face of a multi-sided object).
The visual tokens from SigLIP are projected into the LLM’s embedding space via an MLP connector. In N1 and N1.5, this was a standard two-layer MLP with added layer normalization. In N1.6, the MLP connector was modified to improve performance, and the top four layers of the VLM backbone were unfrozen during pretraining — a deliberate architectural decision to allow the VLM’s upper layers to adapt to the distribution of robot-relevant visual scenes rather than remaining fixed at the internet-data pretraining distribution.
Language Encoder and Cross-Modal Fusion
The Jetson T5000 module powering the AGX Thor Developer Kit includes a Blackwell GPU with 2,560 CUDA cores, 96 fifth-generation Tensor cores, and a 14-core Arm Neoverse-V3AE CPU. Memory is 128 GB of LPDDR5x operating on a 256-bit bus for 276 GB/s of bandwidth. The module is rated for 2,070 TFLOPs at FP4 precision and 1,035 TOPS at FP8. The Blackwell architecture introduces NVFP4 as a first-class inference datatype, enabling 7.5x higher effective AI compute compared to the AGX Orin at the same power envelope, when models are optimized for this format. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) support allows the Blackwell GPU to be partitioned into up to seven independent compute slices, enabling simultaneous execution of the perception stack, the VLM System 2 pass, and the DiT System 1 pass on separate GPU partitions with deterministic resource allocation.
The memory architecture is unified: CPU and GPU draw from the same 128 GB pool with no static partitioning. This eliminates the PCIe bandwidth bottleneck that affects discrete GPU systems when transferring tensors between CPU and GPU memory, which is particularly significant for VLA inference because the pipeline requires frequent data movement between the perception pre-processing stage (often CPU-bound) and the transformer inference stage (GPU-bound).

Quantization and Precision Trade-offs
Running full-precision (BF16 or FP32) VLA models on edge hardware is impractical for most deployments. The GR00T N1.6 3B model uses approximately 6.15 GB of GPU memory in FP16 on a DGX Spark (Blackwell GB10), as documented in community deployment reports. The core challenge of Physical AI lies in this: the physical world is far more complex than the digital world. In the digital world, a flawed inference at most produces imperfect text; in the physical world, one wrong movement can damage equipment, ruin products, or even injure personnel. Robots must make millisecond-level decisions in uncertain environments — perceiving object positions and materials, planning arm trajectories, applying precisely the right amount of force, and adjusting in real time when encountering unexpected situations. This means RT-2 can understand concepts that never appeared in its training data. For example, even without any robot operation examples of "throw trash in the trash can," RT-2 can correctly execute the task based on its semantic understanding of "trash" and "trash can." The implications are profound: it proves robot AI can adopt the "foundation model" paradigm — training one general large model, then fine-tuning for different robot forms, just as GPT can be fine-tuned for text generation in different languages.

A robot simulation platform built on Omniverse. Physical AI Architecture: The Ultimate 2026 VLA Engineering Guide
A deep technical analysis of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures, diffusion-based robot policies, and the infrastructure powering large-scale Physical AI systems.
by
External Sources & Technical References
This article is a technical deep-dive into the architecture and engineering of Physical AI systems in 2026. It covers the internals of Vision-Language-Action models, the full training pipeline from synthetic data generation to sim-to-real transfer, and the inference constraints governing edge deployment on current hardware. All specifications and benchmarks cited are drawn directly from NVIDIA’s published technical documentation, arXiv papers, and official developer blog posts.
TL;DR — Key Insights for AI Engineers
Physical AI is not a single model or framework — it is a multi-layer systems engineering challenge. The core problem is converting noisy, high-dimensional sensor input (RGB frames, depth maps, proprioceptive joint states, IMU readings) into continuous motor commands, in real time, across tasks and environments the system has never seen before. Every component in the stack is constrained by physics: the robot must maintain dynamic balance while manipulating objects, comply with joint torque limits, avoid collisions, and do all of this within the latency budget of a real-time control loop.
Before 2024, the dominant approach was task-specific policy learning: a robot was trained on demonstrations for a single task, in a single environment, with a fixed object set. Generalization was essentially absent. The architectural shift that defines 2025–2026 is the introduction of foundation model backbones into the policy — specifically, large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pretrained on internet-scale data — paired with action generation modules capable of producing smooth, continuous motor trajectories. This is the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) paradigm, and understanding its internals is prerequisite to evaluating any Physical AI platform.
VLA Architecture: Layer-by-Layer
Vision Encoder: SigLIP + MLP Projector
GR00T N1’s visual encoding pipeline begins with a SigLIP vision transformer. SigLIP — Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training — is a contrastive vision encoder trained to produce image representations that are semantically aligned with natural language descriptions. The SigLIP encoder in GR00T N1 operates on image patches of 14×14 pixels. For a standard input resolution, this produces a fixed-length sequence of visual tokens, each with an embedding dimension of 1152. The encoder comprises 27 SiglipEncoderLayer blocks, each containing a SiglipFlashAttention2 self-attention module (with query, key, and value projection dimensions of 1152), followed by layer normalization and a two-layer MLP with GELU activations and a hidden dimension of 4304.
In GR00T N1.6, the VLM was upgraded to a variant of Cosmos-Reason-2B with native resolution support — meaning the vision encoder processes images at their original aspect ratio rather than padding them to a square. This is architecturally significant: padding introduces artificial boundaries in the visual field that the attention mechanism can learn to attend to spuriously, degrading object localization and spatial reasoning. Native resolution support improves scene understanding and task decomposition reliability, particularly for manipulation tasks requiring fine-grained spatial judgment (e.g., grasping a specific face of a multi-sided object).
The visual tokens from SigLIP are projected into the LLM’s embedding space via an MLP connector. In N1 and N1.5, this was a standard two-layer MLP with added layer normalization. In N1.6, the MLP connector was modified to improve performance, and the top four layers of the VLM backbone were unfrozen during pretraining — a deliberate architectural decision to allow the VLM’s upper layers to adapt to the distribution of robot-relevant visual scenes rather than remaining fixed at the internet-data pretraining distribution.
Language Encoder and Cross-Modal Fusion
The Jetson T5000 module powering the AGX Thor Developer Kit includes a Blackwell GPU with 2,560 CUDA cores, 96 fifth-generation Tensor cores, and a 14-core Arm Neoverse-V3AE CPU. Memory is 128 GB of LPDDR5x operating on a 256-bit bus for 276 GB/s of bandwidth. The module is rated for 2,070 TFLOPs at FP4 precision and 1,035 TOPS at FP8. The Blackwell architecture introduces NVFP4 as a first-class inference datatype, enabling 7.5x higher effective AI compute compared to the AGX Orin at the same power envelope, when models are optimized for this format. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) support allows the Blackwell GPU to be partitioned into up to seven independent compute slices, enabling simultaneous execution of the perception stack, the VLM System 2 pass, and the DiT System 1 pass on separate GPU partitions with deterministic resource allocation.
The memory architecture is unified: CPU and GPU draw from the same 128 GB pool with no static partitioning. This eliminates the PCIe bandwidth bottleneck that affects discrete GPU systems when transferring tensors between CPU and GPU memory, which is particularly significant for VLA inference because the pipeline requires frequent data movement between the perception pre-processing stage (often CPU-bound) and the transformer inference stage (GPU-bound).

Quantization and Precision Trade-offs
Running full-precision (BF16 or FP32) VLA models on edge hardware is impractical for most deployments. The GR00T N1.6 3B model uses approximately 6.15 GB of GPU memory in FP16 on a DGX Spark (Blackwell GB10), as documented in community deployment reports. Introduction: The Humanoid Robot Triad of 2026
The year 2026 marks a decisive inflection point in the commercial humanoid robotics landscape. Three platforms dominate the conversation: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas, Tesla’s Optimus (Gen 3), and
Figure AI
’s Figure 02. Each represents a fundamentally different design philosophy, business model, and technical stack. For developers and tech professionals evaluating these systems for integration, research, or deployment, the differences are not merely academic—they dictate feasibility, cost, and capability in real-world environments.
This comparison provides a data-driven, practical analysis of each robot’s hardware specs, software ecosystem, autonomy level, and commercial readiness as of mid-2026.
Hardware Architecture: Actuation, Power, and Payload
Boston Dynamics Atlas (2026 Update)
Atlas remains the most athletically capable humanoid robot ever built. The 2026 iteration sheds its hydraulic system in favor of an advanced electric actuator suite, a move that reduces noise, improves energy efficiency, and lowers maintenance overhead. Key specs include:
Height/Weight:
Tesla Optimus Gen 3 (2026)
Optimus has evolved rapidly from its 2022 prototype. The Gen 3 unit, now in limited production at Tesla’s Fremont facility, prioritizes cost reduction and manufacturability. Key specs:
Height/Weight:
20 kg (arms), 50 kg (squat lift)
Optimus uses a central battery pack mounted in the torso, similar to Tesla vehicles, and leverages the company’s expertise in thermal management and cell chemistry. The hands are a standout feature, capable of handling tools, wires, and small parts with tactile feedback.
Figure 02 (2026 Production Model)
Figure AI, backed by a $1.5B funding round in 2025, has focused on commercial deployment from day one. The Figure 02 is built explicitly for logistics and manufacturing tasks. Key specs:
Height/Weight:
Figure 02’s design emphasizes modularity. The arms, legs, and torso can be replaced in under 30 minutes in the field, a critical advantage for industrial maintenance teams.
Software Stack and Autonomy
Perception and Localization
Atlas:
Relies on a combination of stereo cameras, LiDAR (Velodyne puck), and IMU data. The perception stack is built on a custom ROS 2 framework, with real-time mapping via RTAB-Map. Atlas does not use neural SLAM; it uses explicit geometric mapping for precise foot placement.
Optimus:
Figure 02:
Employs six RGB-D cameras (Intel RealSense) and two Ouster LiDAR units. The software stack runs on a custom NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin-based compute module. Figure uses a hybrid approach: classical motion planning for safety-critical movements and learned policies for manipulation.
Manipulation and Task Execution
Atlas
uses a model-predictive control (MPC) loop running at 1 kHz. Tasks are programmed via offline trajectory optimization and then executed with real-time adaptation. There is no high-level task planner exposed to external developers; Atlas is primarily a research platform.
Optimus
exposes a Python API via Tesla’s custom runtime, allowing developers to script sequences using a high-level action library. The robot can learn new tasks via imitation learning from human demonstrations (teleoperation). In 2026, Tesla released a “Skill Store” where pre-trained manipulation primitives (e.g., “grasp cylinder,” “insert peg”) can be downloaded and composed.
Figure 02
~4,500
Figure 02 leads in real-world deployments, with confirmed installations at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, Amazon Robotics fulfillment centers, and several automotive Tier 1 suppliers. Optimus units are primarily deployed inside Tesla factories—performing bin picking, kitting, and basic assembly tasks. Atlas remains a research platform, though Boston Dynamics has hinted at a commercial Atlas variant for 2027.
Safety and Compliance
Figure 02
offers the most open ecosystem. It provides an official NVIDIA Isaac Sim integration, a Gazebo plugin, and a digital twin API that mirrors the real robot’s state. Figure also publishes a Python SDK with examples for motion planning, perception, and task sequencing. The SDK includes pre-built wrappers for MoveIt 2 and TrajOpt.

Conclusion
In 2026, the humanoid robot market is no longer a single race but three distinct competitions. Boston Dynamics Atlas remains the gold standard for dynamic mobility and research, but it is not a practical tool for most developers or businesses. Tesla Optimus offers the best cost-to-capability ratio for high-volume, repetitive tasks within a controlled environment, leveraging Tesla’s vertical integration and manufacturing scale. Figure 02 provides the most mature, developer-friendly platform for real-world deployment, with a focus on modularity, safety, and open tooling. For technical professionals seeking to integrate humanoid robots into production systems today, Figure 02 is the pragmatic choice. For those pushing the boundaries of locomotion and control, Atlas remains unmatched. Optimus sits in between, promising a future where humanoid robots are as ubiquitous as electric cars—but that future is still a few years away.

Introduction: The Humanoid Robot Triad of 2026
The year 2026 marks a decisive inflection point in the commercial humanoid robotics landscape. Three platforms dominate the conversation: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas, Tesla’s Optimus (Gen 3), and
Figure AI
’s Figure 02. Each represents a fundamentally different design philosophy, business model, and technical stack. For developers and tech professionals evaluating these systems for integration, research, or deployment, the differences are not merely academic—they dictate feasibility, cost, and capability in real-world environments.
This comparison provides a data-driven, practical analysis of each robot’s hardware specs, software ecosystem, autonomy level, and commercial readiness as of mid-2026.
Hardware Architecture: Actuation, Power, and Payload
Boston Dynamics Atlas (2026 Update)
Atlas remains the most athletically capable humanoid robot ever built. The 2026 iteration sheds its hydraulic system in favor of an advanced electric actuator suite, a move that reduces noise, improves energy efficiency, and lowers maintenance overhead. Key specs include:

Optimus uses a central battery pack mounted in the torso, similar to Tesla vehicles, and leverages the company’s expertise in thermal management and cell chemistry. The hands are a standout feature, capable of handling tools, wires, and small parts with tactile feedback.
Figure 02 (2026 Production Model)
Figure AI, backed by a $1.5B funding round in 2025, has focused on commercial deployment from day one. The Figure 02 is built explicitly for logistics and manufacturing tasks. Key specs:

Figure 02’s design emphasizes modularity. The arms, legs, and torso can be replaced in under 30 minutes in the field, a critical advantage for industrial maintenance teams.
Software Stack and Autonomy
Perception and Localization
Atlas:
Relies on a combination of stereo cameras, LiDAR (Velodyne puck), and IMU data. The perception stack is built on a custom ROS 2 framework, with real-time mapping via RTAB-Map. Atlas does not use neural SLAM; it uses explicit geometric mapping for precise foot placement.
Optimus:
Figure 02:
Employs six RGB-D cameras (Intel RealSense) and two Ouster LiDAR units. The software stack runs on a custom NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin-based compute module. Figure uses a hybrid approach: classical motion planning for safety-critical movements and learned policies for manipulation.
Manipulation and Task Execution
Atlas
uses a model-predictive control (MPC) loop running at 1 kHz. Tasks are programmed via offline trajectory optimization and then executed with real-time adaptation. There is no high-level task planner exposed to external developers; Atlas is primarily a research platform.
Optimus
exposes a Python API via Tesla’s custom runtime, allowing developers to script sequences using a high-level action library. The robot can learn new tasks via imitation learning from human demonstrations (teleoperation). In 2026, Tesla released a “Skill Store” where pre-trained manipulation primitives (e.g., “grasp cylinder,” “insert peg”) can be downloaded and composed.
Figure 02
~4,500
Figure 02 leads in real-world deployments, with confirmed installations at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, Amazon Robotics fulfillment centers, and several automotive Tier 1 suppliers. Optimus units are primarily deployed inside Tesla factories—performing bin picking, kitting, and basic assembly tasks. Atlas remains a research platform, though Boston Dynamics has hinted at a commercial Atlas variant for 2027.
Safety and Compliance
Figure 02
offers the most open ecosystem. It provides an official NVIDIA Isaac Sim integration, a Gazebo plugin, and a digital twin API that mirrors the real robot’s state. Figure also publishes a Python SDK with examples for motion planning, perception, and task sequencing. The SDK includes pre-built wrappers for MoveIt 2 and TrajOpt.

Conclusion
In 2026, the humanoid robot market is no longer a single race but three distinct competitions. Boston Dynamics Atlas remains the gold standard for dynamic mobility and research, but it is not a practical tool for most developers or businesses. Tesla Optimus offers the best cost-to-capability ratio for high-volume, repetitive tasks within a controlled environment, leveraging Tesla’s vertical integration and manufacturing scale. Figure 02 provides the most mature, developer-friendly platform for real-world deployment, with a focus on modularity, safety, and open tooling. For technical professionals seeking to integrate humanoid robots into production systems today, Figure 02 is the pragmatic choice. For those pushing the boundaries of locomotion and control, Atlas remains unmatched. Optimus sits in between, promising a future where humanoid robots are as ubiquitous as electric cars—but that future is still a few years away.

장병탁 투모로 로보틱스 대표(우측)와 이정호 레인보우로보틱스 대표(좌측)가 지난 지난 7월 21일 세종특별시에 위치한 레인보우로보틱스 본사에서 ‘Physical AI 기반 로봇 공동개발 및 사업 협력’을 위한 업무 협약을 체결한 뒤 기념 촬영을 하고 있다. 투모로 로보틱스 제공
피지컬 AI(Physical AI) 전문기업 투모로 로보틱스(공동대표 장병탁·박상욱)가 풀스택 로보틱스 기업 레인보우로보틱스(대표이사 이정호)와 손잡고 산업 현장에서 스스로 판단하고 작업을 수행하는 인공지능 기반 휴머노이드 로봇 공동개발(AI-Native)에 나선다. 생성형 AI를 넘어 AI가 현실 공간에서 직접 작업을 수행하는 '피지컬 AI' 상용화에 속도를 내겠다는 구상이다.
투모로 로보틱스는 지난 21일 레인보우로보틱스와 ‘피지컬 AI 기반 로봇 연구개발 및 사업 협력을 위한 업무협약(MOU)’을 체결했다고 23일 밝혔다.
이번 협약은 레인보우로보틱스의 로봇 하드웨어 기술과 투모로 로보틱스의 AI·소프트웨어 기술을 결합해 실제 산업 현장에서 활용할 수 있는 AI-Native 휴머노이드 로봇을 공동 개발하는 것이 핵심이다. 양사는 연구개발을 넘어 현장 실증과 성능 고도화, 고객 발굴, 사업화까지 협력 범위를 확대할 계획이다.
투모로 로보틱스는 로봇 파운데이션 모델(Robot Foundation Model·RFM), AI Agent, 로봇 운영 소프트웨어를 개발·적용하고, 레인보우로보틱스는 로봇 하드웨어와 제어·센서 기술을 지원한다.
양사가 개발하는 AI-Native 로봇은 사람이 미리 입력한 동작을 반복 수행하는 기존 산업용 로봇과 달리 주변 환경과 작업 상황을 스스로 인식하고 판단해 복합 작업을 수행하는 것이 특징이다. 물류센터나 제조 현장에서 물체를 인식해 집고 이동한 뒤 적재하거나 설비를 조작하는 일련의 작업을 하나의 흐름으로 수행하도록 구현하는 것이 목표다.
작업 과정에서 축적되는 데이터는 AI 모델 학습과 로봇 운용 안정성 향상에 다시 활용된다. 장병탁 투모로 로보틱스 공동대표가 앞서 "피지컬 AI는 AI 모델만으로 완성되는 것이 아니라 실제 현장에서 데이터를 반복적으로 확보하고 성능을 개선하는 과정이 중요하다"고 강조한 것처럼, 이번 협력 역시 현장 데이터를 기반으로 AI 성능을 고도화하는 데 초점을 맞췄다.
양사는 ▲로봇 하드웨어와 AI 소프트웨어 연동 및 최적화 ▲산업 현장 실증 과제 발굴과 성능 검증 ▲현장 데이터 기반 로봇 성능 및 운용 안정성 개선 ▲복합 작업 자동화를 위한 AI Agent 개발 ▲공동 고객 발굴 및 사업화 등을 공동 추진한다.
협력은 3단계로 진행된다. 우선 하드웨어와 AI 소프트웨어를 연동해 핵심 인터페이스를 구축하고, 이후 실제 산업 현장 또는 이에 준하는 환경에서 작업 성능과 안정성을 검증한다. 마지막 단계에서는 AI Agent를 활용한 운영 자동화와 WaaS(Workforce-as-a-Service) 사업 모델 적용 가능성을 검토할 예정이다.
WaaS는 기업이 로봇 장비를 직접 구매하는 대신 로봇과 AI 소프트웨어, 운영 시스템을 결합한 '작업 수행 능력'을 서비스 형태로 제공받는 개념이다. 피킹과 이송, 분류, 검사 등 특정 작업을 서비스로 이용할 수 있는 새로운 사업 모델이다.
실증 과정에서는 반복 작업의 안정성과 작업 처리 시간, 안전성, 장애 대응 능력, 운영 편의성 등을 종합적으로 검증한다. 양사는 실증 결과를 바탕으로 기술을 지속적으로 고도화하고 공동 제안과 데모, 전시, 상용 프로젝트 등으로 협력을 확대할 계획이다.

Software Architecture: The New Bottleneck for Physical AI
header-teaser, header-teaser-item-box-position-left, header-teaser-item-box-color-dark, enable-dynamic-media
Robotics is experiencing an unprecedented era of innovation, driven by the rapid rise of Physical AI and machine learning capabilities. As robots increasingly break out of controlled factory cages and navigate dynamic human environments, traditional development paradigms are shifting. According to the newly released
Inside the Robot: Architecture Benchmark Report
by QNX, which surveyed 1,000 global robotics developers, hardware is no longer the primary constraint. Today, software has taken the lead: almost one in three developers (27%) cite software architecture and integration as their biggest performance bottleneck, compared to just 16% who cite hardware constraints.
Here is a breakdown of the core findings and what they mean for the future of robotics engineering.
The Physical AI Imperative vs. Real-World Readiness
The ambition across the robotics sector is clear. Nearly nine in ten developers (89%) view Physical AI, systems that can perceive, reason, and act autonomously in the physical world, as critical to their organizational strategy over the next three to five years. To support this transition,
85% of developers expect the role of software to expand
, with development teams anticipating their largest future budget allocations will go toward AI-driven decision making (51%) and cybersecurity (51%).
However, ambition is currently outpacing field readiness. While industry optimism remains highly resilient, only 29% of developers feel "very confident" in their systems' ability to make safe, predictable decisions in unconstrained, real-world environments.
The Determinism Disconnect: Flexibility vs. Safety
As robotics systems increasingly operate alongside humans, a reality for 83% of respondents today, the demand for flawless reliability skyrockets. An overwhelming
95% of developers state that deterministic, real-time execution is essential
91% of development teams still rely on general-purpose operating systems (GPOS)
, such as Linux, to run at least some real-time or safety-critical workloads. Nearly a third (32%) do so extensively.
To manage this, 64% of businesses currently utilize hybrid architectures that combine safety controllers, vision computers, and microcontrollers. While these hybrid setups enhance capability, they significantly increase integration complexity, which 42% of developers cite as their biggest software development challenge
.
The Certification Wall
The tension between utilizing flexible, open-source software and meeting strict industry safety guarantees is resulting in massive deployment bottlenecks. Two-thirds (66%) of developers report experiencing project delays specifically due to industry certification requirements. This friction is heavily tied to two main regulatory hurdles: cybersecurity standards (such as ISO/SAE 21434) and functional safety standards (like ISO 10218), which are cited as the most challenging to navigate by 51% and 49% of respondents, respectively.
The commercial and financial pressure to push through these bottlenecks is immense. Alarmingly, 84% of developers agree that strict deadlines and budget pressures can lead engineering teams to compromise on critical aspects of development, including safety protocols.
Implications: Re-evaluating the Foundation
The robotics industry is rapidly approaching an architectural tipping point. Scaling Physical AI requires foundational software that can handle mixed-criticality workloads safely, without crippling development velocity or risking failed compliance audits.
Recognizing the limits of their current stacks,
86% of respondents currently using a GPOS express openness to changing their operating system
. When looking ahead to mitigate integration and scalability limits, many developers are shifting toward more robust paradigms: 31% cite a safety-certified commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) operating system as the best fit for their needs, while 27% are opting for virtualized Linux combined with a Real-Time OS (RTOS).
Conclusion
Hardware advances have set the stage, but the next major leap in robotics will be dictated by software architecture. Re-evaluating foundational architectures from the OS up is no longer just a backend technical exercise; it is a strategic necessity for securing certifications, ensuring human safety, and successfully scaling Physical AI into the real world.

Abstract:
Amid growing efforts to leverage advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for robotics, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently gained significant attention. By unifying vision, language, and action data at scale, which have traditionally been studied separately, VLA models aim to learn policies that generalise across diverse tasks, objects, embodiments, and environments. This generalisation capability is expected to enable robots to solve novel downstream tasks with minimal or no additional task-specific data, facilitating more flexible and scalable real-world deployment. Unlike previous surveys that focus narrowly on action representations or high-level model architectures, this work offers a comprehensive, full-stack review, integrating both software and hardware components of VLA systems. In particular, this paper provides a systematic review of VLAs, covering their strategy and architectural transition, architectures and building blocks, modality-specific processing techniques, and learning paradigms. In addition, to support the deployment of VLAs in real-world robotic applications, we also review commonly used robot platforms, data collection strategies, publicly available datasets, data augmentation methods, and evaluation benchmarks. Throughout this comprehensive survey, this paper aims to offer practical guidance for the robotics community in applying VLAs to real-world robotic systems. 차세대 인공지능과 액추에이터 융합해 지능형 로봇 시장 선점에 나선다
삼성전자가 2026년 9월 7일 차세대 지능형 휴머노이드(인간형 로봇) 개발 프로젝트를 본격화하고 2027년 1월 미국 라스베이거스에서 열리는 세계 최대 전자·정보기술 전시회 CES 2027 공개를 목표로 실무 작업에 착수했다. 글로벌 빅테크 기업들이 생성형 인공지능(AI)과 로봇 공학을 결합한 지능형 로봇 개발에 속도를 내는 가운데 반도체와 소프트웨어, 가전 생태계를 두루 갖춘 종합 전자 기업의 제조 역량을 로봇 하드웨어에 이식하려는 시도다.
인간의 신체적 특성을 모사한 휴머노이드 개발은 최근 산업 현장과 가정 내 서비스 영역 모두에서 차세대 전략 산업으로 급부상하고 있다. 테슬라가 자체 개발 중인 옵티머스를 연이어 개량하고 있고 피규어AI와 보스턴다이내믹스 같은 전문 로봇 제조사들도 첨단 센서와 신경망을 탑재한 시제품을 연달아 공개했다. 로봇 시장의 무게중심이 고정된 위치에서 정밀 작업을 수행하던 전통적 산업용 다관절 로봇에서 자율적으로 환경을 인식하고 행동하는 지능형 개체로 급격히 전환되는 추세다.
휴머노이드 로봇은 머리 부분에 장착된 3차원 비전 센서와 라이다(LiDAR·빛 탐지 및 거리 측정)를 통해 주변 지형을 입체적으로 인식한다. 로봇의 관절에는 회전력을 정밀하게 제어하는 초소형 모터와 감속기가 결합한 액추에이터(구동 장치)가 탑재되어 두 발로 균형을 잡으며 걷거나 계단을 오르내리는 동작을 수행한다. 사람의 손가락 구조를 본뜬 매니퓰레이터(로봇 손)는 수많은 촉각 센서와 힘 피드백 알고리즘을 활용해 달걀처럼 깨지기 쉬운 물체를 깨뜨리지 않고 쥐거나 미세한 전자기 부품을 조립하는 정밀 작업을 지원한다.
글로벌 조사기관 인터내셔널데이터코퍼레이션(IDC)에 따르면 전 세계 인공지능 및 로봇 융합 시장 규모는 2024년 420억 달러 수준에서 연평균 25% 이상 성장해 2030년 1600억 달러를 넘어설 것으로 집계됐다. 로봇의 두뇌에 해당하는 인공지능 모델이 거대언어모델(LLM)과 멀티모달(복합정보처리) 기술을 흡수하면서 로봇이 사람의 자연어 명령을 듣고 스스로 행동 순서를 계획하는 단계로 발전한 결과다. 공장 내 단순 반복 작업을 넘어 물류 분류와 노인 돌봄, 매장 안내 등 복합적인 판단이 요구되는 환경으로 로봇의 활동 반경이 넓어지고 있다.
반도체와 온디바이스(기기 탑재형) AI 분야에서 축적한 기술 자산은 로봇 설계에 직접 활용된다. 인간형 로봇이 시각 정보와 센서 데이터를 지연 없이 처리하려면 초저전력 고성능 신경망처리장치(NPU)가 필수적이다. 클라우드 서버와의 통신 지연을 최소화하고 로봇 내부에서 실시간으로 관절 각도와 보행 궤적을 연산하기 위해 기기 자체에서 구동되는 고효율 엣지 컴퓨팅 하드웨어가 두뇌 역할을 맡는다. 배터리 용량의 한계 속에서 장시간 구동을 보장하기 위해서는 전력 관리 반도체(PMIC)와 모바일 프로세서 설계 기술의 집약이 요구된다.
로봇 하드웨어 부문에서는 고출력 밀도를 갖춘 모터와 하모닉 드라이브 감속기를 소형화하는 기술이 핵심 과제로 꼽힌다. 인간의 체형과 무게를 크게 벗어나지 않으면서도 수십 킬로그램의 하중을 들어 올리려면 관절 단위의 열 방출 설계와 토크(회전력) 제어의 정밀도가 담보되어야 한다. 이를 위해 외부 충격에 유연하게 반응하는 준직접구동(QDD) 방식 액추에이터와 정밀 역학 센서가 관절마다 배치되며, 경량 복합 알루미늄과 탄소 섬유 복합 소재를 사용해 전체 하중을 줄이는 작업이 병행된다.
한국로봇산업진흥원은 최근 보고서에서 국내 로봇 부품 국산화율이 소프트웨어 플랫폼과 구동 제어기 분야에서 꾸준히 상승하고 있으며, 감속기와 서보모터 등 핵심 하드웨어 분야에서도 국산 대체 기술이 점진적으로 확보되고 있다고 분석했다. 정부 역시 첨단 로봇 산업 비전과 전략을 수립하고 제조 현장 내 지능형 로봇 보급률을 끌어올리기 위한 실증 사업과 규제 개선을 이어오고 있다. 공공 인프라와 민간 실증 단지를 연계해 휴머노이드의 주행 안전성과 작업 신뢰성을 검증하는 시험대가 전국 주요 산업단지에서 운영되는 중이다.
협회 관계자는 "단순한 기계적 균형 제어를 넘어 주변 상황을 시각적으로 이해하고 다음 행동을 예측하는 피지컬 AI(물리적 인공지능) 역량이 향후 로봇 산업의 승패를 결정짓는 핵심 지표가 될 것"이라며 "세계적인 수준의 반도체 공정과 대규모 양산 체계를 갖춘 종합 정보기술 기업의 진입은 글로벌 휴머노이드 상용화 시점을 대폭 앞당기는 분기점이 된다"고 설명했다. 이 관계자는 이어 "기존 스마트폰이나 가전 기기와의 연동성까지 확보된다면 산업용 라인뿐만 아니라 주거 공간에서도 강력한 플랫폼 지배력을 형성할 수 있다"고 밝혔다.
국내 부품 제조사들 사이에서도 공급망 다변화에 대한 기대감이 형성되고 있다. 대구의 한 로봇 감속기 협력사에서 기술 개발을 총괄하는 최모 씨(49)는 "그동안 정밀 감속기나 엔코더 같은 핵심 구동 부품은 해외 수입 의존도가 높아 납기와 단가 조절에 큰 제약이 따랐다"며 "국내 대표 전자 기업이 주도하는 차세대 휴머노이드 프로젝트가 실체화되면 국산 정밀 모터와 특수 감속기를 공급할 수 있는 판로가 열려 국내 부품 생태계 전반의 자생력이 강화된다"고 말했다.
소프트웨어 분야에서는 디지털 트윈(가상 모형) 환경을 활용한 가상 학습이 집중적으로 이뤄진다. 수백만 대의 가상 로봇을 시뮬레이터 공간에 배치해 물리 법칙에 기반한 강화학습을 거치게 함으로써 실제 기계 부품의 마모나 파손 없이 수만 시간 분량의 보행 및 파지(물체 쥐기) 데이터를 축적한다. 엔비디아의 옴니버스나 아이작 심 같은 로봇 전용 시뮬레이터를 기반으로 가상 환경에서 학습된 신경망 모델을 실제 로봇에 이식하는 심투리얼(Sim-to-Real) 전환 기술이 개발 속도를 끌어올리는 원동력이다.
국제표준화기구(ISO)는 서비스 로봇과 휴머노이드의 안전 규격을 제정하기 위해 협동로봇 안전 기준인 ISO 10218 및 개인 지원 로봇 안전 표준인 ISO 13482 개정 작업을 진행하고 있다. 로봇이 인간과 같은 공간에서 물리적으로 상호작용할 때 발생할 수 있는 충돌 위험을 감지하고 모터 출력을 순간적으로 차단하거나 회피 기동을 취하도록 강제하는 기능 안전성 기준이 점차 고도화되는 상황이다. 인체 접촉 시 가해지는 압력을 일정 한도 이하로 유지하도록 설계하는 안전 제어 소프트웨어 탑재가 필수 요건으로 자리 잡고 있다.
산업통상자원부는 2024년부터 2028년까지 추진하는 제4차 지능형 로봇 기본계획을 바탕으로 로봇 핵심 부품과 소프트웨어 국산화 지원 예산을 지속해서 투입하고 있다. 감속기, 서보모터, 그리퍼, 센서, 제어기 등 로봇 5대 핵심 부품의 자립도를 높이고 인공지능 반도체와 통신 칩셋을 하나로 묶는 온디바이스 로봇 통합 모듈 개발을 국가 연구개발 과제로 지정해 운영 중이다. 물류 창고와 반도체 클린룸 등 고정밀 작업 현장을 중심으로 인간형 로봇의 초기 실증 수요를 창출하는 정책적 뒷받침도 병행된다.
통계청이 발표한 국내 제조업 노동력 현황에 따르면 생산 가능 인구 감소로 인해 정밀 조립 및 물류 공정에서의 인력 수급 격차가 매년 심화되고 있다. 산업 현장에서는 인력 부족 문제를 해결하고 작업자의 근골격계 질환을 예방하기 위해 반복적이고 중량물을 다루는 공정에 인간형 로봇을 도입하려는 수요가 가파르게 늘고 있다. 정형화된 컨베이어 벨트를 벗어나 유연하게 작업 구역을 이동하며 다품종 소량 생산 공정을 도맡아 처리할 수 있는 유연성이 인간형 로봇의 가장 큰 강점으로 평가된다.
연구위원은 "인간형 로봇이 공장 바닥을 벗어나 실생활 공간에 안착하려면 전력 소모를 획기적으로 낮추는 모빌리티 메커니즘과 더불어 뜻밖의 돌발 변수에 즉각 대응하는 상식 수준의 인공지능 추론 능력이 결합되어야 한다"며 "제조 단가를 낮추는 대량 양산 기술과 부품 신뢰성 검증 과정이 남아 있는 만큼 상용화 직전 단계까지 엄격한 안정성 시험이 요구된다"고 밝혔다.
미국가전협회(CTA)는 매년 1월 미국 네바다주 라스베이거스 컨벤션센터에서 개최되는 CES의 공식 기조연설과 전시 주제로 인공지능과 로보틱스의 융합을 집중 조명하고 있다. 주요 글로벌 제조사들은 CES 2027 본무대를 겨냥해 차세대 지능형 로봇의 실물 시연과 산업 적용 청사진을 발표하기 위한 사전 기술 검증을 진행 중이다.

Samsung Builds AI Into Robot Design to Speed Humanoid Push
[Samsung Humanoid to Debut at CES Next Year]

Factories used as large-scale data collection bases

Samsung Bot Handy uses a duster to clean dust inside a home (left); Samsung Bot Handy grips a cup (right). Samsung Electronics
Samsung Electronics (005930) is accelerating in-house development of humanoid robots on an internal assessment that advances in artificial intelligence and the commercialization of physical AI are arriving faster than expected, according to industry sources. Domestic rivals are moving as well: Hyundai Motor (005380) Group has unveiled a new Atlas, and LG Group has introduced Cloi'd, both positioning to claim the humanoid market early. Chinese companies, meanwhile, are scaling up humanoids at a formidable pace in the global market. To counter rivals' speed and volume, Samsung has set a goal of internalizing everything from product design to the AI brain and seizing leadership of the humanoid industry ecosystem at a stroke.
Yoon Jang-hyun, president and chief technology officer of the DX Division. Samsung Electronics
Samsung's push shows first in an unconventional organizational setup. In the Robotics (RX) Business Promotion Office created in July, Yoon Jang-hyun, president and chief technology officer of the Device eXperience (DX) division, concurrently heads both the hardware development team and the AI software development team. It is unusual at a large corporation for a single executive to oversee both the hardware organization handling robot drivetrains and the AI organization building perception and autonomous navigation.
The industry reads this as shifting the lead in robot development from hardware to AI and software. The old approach of building a mechanical frame first and layering software on top cannot keep up with AI advances that change by the day. Executives therefore appear to have given Yoon, a software specialist, full authority over development to build a custom humanoid optimized for AI algorithms from the initial design stage, sharply shortening the development period and raising the level of completion. The aim is to eliminate the development gap between the brain and the body and bring out a product at commercial readiness right away.
Samsung has been methodically securing core technologies and trademarks for its own robots for years. On trademarks, it filed early for "SAMSUNG BOT" in 2022 to lock in rights. That led the industry to expect Samsung Bot would be the name of the company's next-generation robot brand.
The company also filed in 2024 for humanoid hip joint design technology, which determines the success of bipedal walking, securing its own lower-body structure. In April this year, it registered a next-generation robot hand patent in the United States that combines camera vision to flexibly rearrange finger configurations according to the shape of an object. Adding language-model control technology that converts natural-language instructions into physical motion completed the technical puzzle.
A dual research structure linking the R&D campus in Umyeon-dong, Seoul, with the Gumi plant in North Gyeongsang Province is seen as a distinctive Samsung strength. At the Umyeon-dong campus, Samsung Electronics is demonstrating core brain technologies such as visual recognition and precision control for humanoids and refining them. Technology developed there is applied directly to a "data factory" under construction at sites including the Gumi plant for validation.
For robots to work adeptly in the physical world, vast amounts of physical data are needed. Samsung, which operates semiconductor, smartphone and home appliance production lines around the world, can use its own factories as a huge data collection base. That is an overwhelming comparative advantage that global big tech firms relying on laboratory simulations would find hard to match in a short time.
Samsung Electronics is moving quickly on robots because the global robot market is growing rapidly. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global humanoid market is projected to expand from 6.6 trillion won in 2025 to 222.4 trillion won in 2034. It has emerged from a niche into a vast market that could decide the fate of future manufacturing.
China has taken early leadership in this fast-growing robot market. According to market research firm Smart Analytics Global, global humanoid shipments reached 19,100 units in the first half of this year, a 272% surge from a year earlier. Strikingly, Chinese companies accounted for more than 97% of global shipments in the period. Agibot led with 8,400 units delivered in the first half for a 44% global share, followed by Unitree at 31%, Galbot at 5%, UBTech at 4% and LEJU at 3%.
Chinese robots are seen as having moved past simple proof-of-concept work into mass production, deployed directly on automobile assembly and parts production lines. Smart Analytics Global estimated that more than 70% of first-half humanoid shipments went into industrial and commercial use.
Many analysts say the recent tightening of U.S. restrictions on imports of Chinese products is a decisive opportunity for Samsung and other Korean companies.

표면을 따라 미세한 진동과 함께 작업이 시작됐다. 별도 설계 도면이나 사전 입력 없이도 로봇은 구조물의 형상을 스스로 스캔하고 곧바로 최적의 경로를 그리듯 움직였다.

스캔앤고는 협동로봇 팔과 자율이동로봇(AMR)을 결합한 플랫폼에 물리정보 기반 AI와 3D 비전 기술을 적용한 산업용 AI 로봇 솔루션이다. 대형 구조물 형상을 스스로 인식하고 최적의 작업 경로를 생성해 검사, 샌딩, 그라인딩 등 작업을 자동 수행한다.
이 솔루션은 터빈 블레이드, 항공기 동체, 건물 외벽 등 대형 복합 구조물의 표면을 스캔한 뒤 별도의 설계 도면 없이 작업을 수행하는 것이 특징이다. 플러그앤플레이 방식으로 운영돼 현장 적용성이 높고, 0.1mm 수준의 작업 정밀도를
구현했다.
로봇팔 6개 축에 장착된 토크센서를 통해 작업 대상이 달라져도 실시간 힘 제어가 가능하며, 산업용 안전 기준인 PLe, Cat4도 충족했다.

Title:

Authors:
Yu Feng

View PDF
Abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a key component in embodied AI. Among existing approaches, diffusion-based VLA models achieve superior motion quality and generalization. However, diffusion-based VLA models are compute-intensive and must run at high control frequency, e.g., 50-200 Hz. Thus, it imposes strict latency and energy constraints on edge devices.
In this work, we present Deltoris, an algorithm-hardware co-design framework for efficient diffusion-based VLA inference. First, we exploit the temporal similarity of consecutive inputs and propose a \textit{temporal-aware bit-sparsity} algorithm that computes only the differences between consecutive inputs, eliminating redundant bit-level operations. To further address the extra off-chip traffic introduced by our algorithm, we propose a \textit{speculative inference} technique, which amortizes data loading across multiple control steps. Lastly, to support these techniques, we co-design a dedicated accelerator with customized 1D systolic bit-serial PE arrays that eliminate PE workload imbalance. Our evaluation shows that Deltoris achieves up to 34.2$\times$ speedup over mobile GPUs and 6.1$\times$ over prior accelerators, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

Title:
VLA-RAIL: A Real-Time Asynchronous Inference Linker for VLA Models and Robots
Authors:
Han Gao
View a PDF of the paper titled VLA-RAIL: A Real-Time Asynchronous Inference Linker for VLA Models and Robots, by Yongsheng Zhao and 5 other authors
View PDF
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable breakthroughs in robotics, with the action chunk playing a dominant role in these advances. Given the real-time and continuous nature of robotic motion control, the strategies for fusing a queue of successive action chunks have a profound impact on the overall performance of VLA models. Existing methods suffer from jitter, stalling, or even pauses in robotic action execution, which not only limits the achievable execution speed but also reduces the overall success rate of task completion. This paper introduces VLA-RAIL (A Real-Time Asynchronous Inference Linker), a novel framework designed to address these issues by conducting model inference and robot motion control asynchronously and guaranteeing smooth, continuous, and high-speed action execution. The core contributions of the paper are two fold: a Trajectory Smoother that effectively filters out the noise and jitter in the trajectory of one action chunk using polynomial fitting and a Chunk Fuser that seamlessly align the current executing trajectory and the newly arrived chunk, ensuring position, velocity, and acceleration continuity between two successive action chunks. We validate the effectiveness of VLA-RAIL on a benchmark of dynamic simulation tasks and several real-world manipulation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VLA-RAIL significantly reduces motion jitter, enhances execution speed, and improves task success rates, which will become a key infrastructure for the large-scale deployment of VLA models.

According to IEEE Spectrum, 2025 was supposed to be the year AI and humanoid robots made transformative progress toward real practicality. The money arrived. The hype was everywhere. But as IEEE Spectrum reported, it became genuinely hard to rationalize what actually happened against the scale of investment and optimism heading into the year. That gap between capital and capability points directly at hardware. Not software. Not AI. The actuator stack, the thermal budget, and the sensing architecture are where humanoid development keeps stalling. ActuatorHQ analysis: this is exactly why component-level thinking matters. A better foundation model does not fix a joint that overheats after 20 minutes of operation.

Stable bipedal locomotion demands real-time sensor fusion, complex dynamic modelling, and continuous feedback across dozens of degrees of freedom simultaneously.
According to the Wiley Knowledge Hub technical examination of humanoid engineering challenges, motion control remains the single hardest unsolved problem in the field. The reasons are layered. Maintaining stable bipedal locomotion across dynamic environments requires managing modelling complexity, real-time feedback requirements, and sensor fusion demands all at once. Every joint in a humanoid leg or arm is a potential failure point under load. The number of degrees of freedom in a full humanoid, typically ranging from 20 to more than 40 active joints, means the control system must coordinate an enormous number of actuator states in real time. Any lag, any miscalibration, any thermal drift in a sensor signal, and the robot falls.

What role does sensor fusion play at the joint level?
The Wiley technical brief highlights inertial measurement units, force and torque feedback, and tactile sensing as the core sensing modalities for reliable human-robot interaction and collision avoidance. Fusing these streams in real time while driving 20-plus joints is a compute and latency problem as much as a mechanical one. Actuator designers who integrate force-torque sensing directly into the joint housing are reducing the signal path length and improving fusion latency.

How do power and thermal constraints determine operational endurance?
Battery chemistry selection between LFP and NCA, DC/DC converter topology choices, and thermal protection strategies directly set the ceiling on how long a humanoid can operate.
The Wiley Knowledge Hub technical examination goes specific on power system design in a way that most humanoid coverage ignores. The trade-off between lithium iron phosphate chemistry (LFP) and nickel cobalt aluminum chemistry (NCA) is not academic. LFP offers better thermal stability and cycle life. NCA offers higher energy density. For a humanoid carrying its own power, that chemistry decision affects both runtime and how aggressively you can push the actuator stack before the battery becomes a thermal risk. On top of chemistry, DC/DC converter topology selection shapes how efficiently power is distributed across joints under dynamic load conditions.

Do you optimize for safety margins and longevity, or for energy density and peak performance? Teams building for industrial deployment are likely weighting LFP more heavily. Why does thermal management deserve its own engineering track?
Thermal protection strategy is listed as a distinct design variable in the Wiley technical brief, separate from battery and converter decisions. This matters because actuator motors generate heat under load, and in a compact humanoid body the heat paths are constrained. An actuator that performs well at ambient temperature in a lab may throttle or fault after sustained operation in a warm warehouse. Thermal design at the joint level is not optional at production scale.
What does the shift to modular architectures mean for actuator design?
Modular architecture is the industry response to production scaling pressure, pushing actuator designers to standardize interfaces, thermal profiles, and control protocols across joint families.
The Wiley Knowledge Hub technical brief identifies the shift toward modular architectures as a defining transition as humanoid development moves from prototype to mass production. From an actuator perspective, this is significant. Prototype hardware can be bespoke and hand-tuned. Production hardware needs to be swappable, manufacturable at volume, and consistent across units. Modular actuator design means standardized mechanical interfaces, predictable thermal envelopes, and interoperable communication protocols. It is a fundamentally different design discipline from building a one-off demo joint. The companies that solve modular actuator design early will have a structural manufacturing cost advantage.
